subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of electric current?
questions.explain: Electric current is measured in amperes (amps), symbol A.

questions.q: Which instrument measures current and how is it connected in a circuit?
questions.explain: An ammeter is placed in series so the same current it measures flows through it.

questions.q: How should a voltmeter be connected to measure the potential difference across a lamp?
options: In parallel, across the battery only
questions.explain: A voltmeter is connected in parallel across the component to measure the p.d. between its ends.

questions.q: Which equation correctly relates charge, current and time?
questions.explain: Charge (coulombs) equals current (amperes) multiplied by time (seconds), Q = It.

questions.q: A current of 2 A flows for 5 s. How much charge passes a point in the circuit?
questions.explain: Using Q = It gives 2 × 5 = 10 coulombs.

questions.q: What is the unit of resistance and how is it defined?
questions.explain: Resistance is measured in ohms and defined as R = V/I.

questions.q: A current of 3 A flows through a 4 Ω resistor. What is the potential difference across it?
questions.explain: Using V = IR gives 3 × 4 = 12 volts.

questions.q: For a metallic conductor kept at constant temperature, how do current and potential difference relate?
options: Current is directly proportional to potential difference
Current is inversely proportional to potential difference
Current stays constant as p.d. increases
questions.explain: An ohmic conductor at constant temperature shows current directly proportional to p.d., giving a straight line through the origin.

questions.q: What happens to the resistance of a metal filament lamp as it gets hotter?
options: The resistance stays exactly the same
questions.explain: As the filament heats up its resistance increases, so its current-voltage graph curves.

questions.q: In a series circuit, what is true about the current?
options: It is the same at every point in the circuit
It is largest nearest the battery
It is different across each component
questions.explain: There is only one path in a series circuit, so the current is the same everywhere.

questions.q: How is the total resistance of two resistors connected in series found?
options: By adding the individual resistances together
By taking the smaller of the two values
By dividing the larger value by the smaller
questions.explain: For resistors in series the total resistance is the sum of the separate resistances.

questions.q: In a parallel circuit, what is true about the potential difference across each branch?
options: It is the same across each branch and equals the supply p.d.
It is shared equally so each branch gets less
It is zero across each branch
questions.explain: Components in parallel all have the same p.d. across them, equal to the supply voltage.

questions.q: A 3 Ω resistor and a 5 Ω resistor are connected in series. What is their total resistance?
questions.explain: In series the resistances add: 3 + 5 = 8 Ω.

questions.q: At a junction in a parallel circuit, how do the branch currents relate to the main current?
options: The branch currents add up to the main current
Each branch carries the full main current
The branch currents multiply to give the main current
The main current is the largest single branch current
questions.explain: Current is conserved, so the currents in the parallel branches sum to the total current from the supply.

questions.q: What are the voltage and frequency of the UK mains electricity supply?
questions.explain: UK mains is supplied at about 230 volts with a frequency of 50 hertz.

questions.q: Which type of current does the mains supply provide?
questions.explain: Mains electricity is alternating current, which repeatedly reverses direction.

questions.q: What is the colour of the earth wire in a UK three-pin plug?
questions.explain: The earth wire is green and yellow; live is brown and neutral is blue.

questions.q: In which wire of a mains appliance is the fuse fitted, and why?
options: The live wire, so it disconnects the appliance from the high voltage if too much current flows
The neutral wire, so the appliance stays at earth potential
The earth wire, so it carries the fault current safely
Any wire, because the position does not matter
questions.explain: The fuse is placed in the live wire so that if it blows the appliance is isolated from the dangerous live supply.

questions.q: Which equation gives the electrical power transferred by a device?
questions.explain: Electrical power is calculated using P = VI (voltage multiplied by current).

questions.q: An appliance operates at 230 V and draws a current of 2 A. What is its power?
questions.explain: Using P = VI gives 230 × 2 = 460 watts.
